title: Divide Two Integers
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated subtraction versus doubling-based chunk removal, then a single clean pass over the quotient's bits.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given two integers, dividend and divisor, compute their integer division truncated toward zero, without using multiplication, division, or modulo.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two numbers, dividend and divisor, compute their integer division, truncated toward zero, without using the multiplication, division, or modulo operators.

blocks.title: Analogy: Pouring Liquid With Only a Set of Cups
blocks.text: Picture measuring out a large amount of liquid using only a set of identical cups, with no scale and no way to multiply. The fastest way is not to pour one cup at a time, counting endlessly, it is to grab the biggest matching container you have (a jug worth 2 cups, then 4 cups, then 8), pour out as many of the biggest container as still fit, then switch to a smaller one for what remains. This problem is exactly that: finding how many times the divisor fits into the dividend, without ever multiplying.

blocks.caption: Subtract chunks of the divisor to build up the quotient

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: dividend = 10, divisor = 3

Example: dividend = 0, divisor = 1
Zero divided by anything is 0.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what tools are actually still available without multiplication or division.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Without multiplication or division available, the only tools left to combine numbers are addition, subtraction, and bit shifts, so the quotient has to be built up from repeated subtraction in some form.

Observation 2: Subtracting the divisor one copy at a time correctly counts how many times it fits, but does so at the slowest possible rate, one unit of the quotient per subtraction.

Observation 3: A left bit shift doubles a number without ever calling a multiplication operator, so doubling the chunk being subtracted, and doubling how much that chunk represents, removes exponentially larger pieces of the dividend at once instead of linearly.

Observation 4: Carried to its natural conclusion, this doubling idea can be restructured into deciding each bit of the final quotient directly, from the most significant bit down to the least, in one single clean pass instead of a nested loop.
That reasoning alone already sketches the whole path: replace one-at-a-time subtraction with doubling, then collapse the doubling into a single bit-by-bit pass.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most direct approach, without multiplication or division, is to repeatedly subtract the divisor from the dividend, one copy at a time, counting how many subtractions happen before the dividend drops below the divisor.
Step by step algorithm

items: Determine the sign of the result from whether the dividend and divisor have matching or differing signs.
Work with the absolute values of both numbers from here on.
While the dividend is still at least the divisor, subtract the divisor once and increase a counter.
Apply the sign determined earlier to the final counter.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: subtract one copy of the divisor at a time

codes.python:
def divide(dividend, divisor):
    negative = (dividend < 0) != (divisor < 0)   # result is negative if signs differ
    dividend, divisor = abs(dividend), abs(divisor)
    quotient = 0
    while dividend >= divisor:
        dividend -= divisor       # subtract one copy of the divisor at a time
        quotient += 1               # count each subtraction
    return -quotient if negative else quotient


if __name__ == "__main__":
    dividend, divisor = 10, 3
    print(divide(dividend, divisor))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The sign of the result is determined once, up front, by comparing whether the dividend and divisor's signs differ, specifically so the rest of the logic can work entirely with absolute values and never worry about sign again until the very end.
Working with absolute values throughout avoids subtle bugs from mixing positive and negative comparisons inside the subtraction loop, which only ever needs to compare two non-negative magnitudes.

The sign is reapplied to the final quotient as the very last step, after the counting loop has finished, rather than tracked alongside the count throughout, keeping the counting logic itself completely sign agnostic.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because repeatedly subtracting the divisor and counting each subtraction reconstructs exactly how many whole copies of the divisor fit into the dividend.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(dividend divided by divisor), one subtraction per unit of the quotient.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: for extreme inputs, like dividing 2 billion by 1, this approach needs roughly 2 billion individual subtractions, far too slow. Subtracting only one copy of the divisor at a time wastes an enormous amount of work whenever much larger chunks could safely be removed at once.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why subtracting one copy at a time works but is far too slow: for an extreme case like dividing 2 billion by 1, this needs roughly 2 billion individual subtractions before finishing.

What is being wasted: every single subtraction only ever removes exactly one divisor's worth, even when the remaining dividend could easily absorb a much bigger chunk at once.

Can a bigger chunk be found without multiplying: yes, repeatedly left-shifting the divisor doubles it each time, a chunk that grows exponentially while still only using bitwise operations.

How large should that chunk be allowed to grow: as large as possible while still fitting within what remains of the dividend, found by doubling it until doubling again would overshoot.

The core idea: find the largest doubled chunk of the divisor that still fits, subtract it all at once, and credit the quotient for the whole chunk in one step.

Instead of subtracting one copy of the divisor at a time, double the amount being subtracted using a left bit shift (equivalent to multiplying by 2, without using multiplication) for as long as it still fits within the remaining dividend, then subtract that whole doubled chunk at once.
This removes huge chunks of the dividend in each outer step instead of one unit at a time.
9. Optimized Solution

For each pass, start with the divisor itself and keep doubling it (and tracking how many divisors that doubled value represents) as long as the doubled value still fits in the remaining dividend. Subtract the largest chunk found, add its represented count to the quotient, and repeat from the top.
Dry run for dividend = 43, divisor = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pass","Largest chunk subtracted","Multiple added to quotient","Remaining dividend","Why"],"rows":[["1","24 (3 shifted left 3 times)","8","19","Doubling 3 to 6, 12, 24 all still fit within 43, but doubling once more to 48 would not."],["2","12 (3 shifted left 2 times)","4","7","Against the smaller remaining dividend of 19, doubling only reaches 12 before overshooting."],["3","6 (3 shifted left 1 time)","2","1","Against 7, doubling only reaches 6 before overshooting."]]}

blocks.text: The quotient accumulates 8 + 4 + 2 = 14, and 1 remains, which is discarded since this is integer division.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: double the chunk being subtracted for as long as it still fits

codes.python:
def divide(dividend, divisor):
    negative = (dividend < 0) != (divisor < 0)
    dividend, divisor = abs(dividend), abs(divisor)
    quotient = 0
    while dividend >= divisor:
        temp_divisor, multiple = divisor, 1
        while dividend >= (temp_divisor << 1):
            temp_divisor <<= 1          # double the chunk we are about to subtract
            multiple <<= 1                # double how much that chunk counts for
        dividend -= temp_divisor        # remove the largest chunk that still fit
        quotient += multiple              # credit the quotient for that whole chunk at once
    return -quotient if negative else quotient


if __name__ == "__main__":
    dividend, divisor = 10, 3
    print(divide(dividend, divisor))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because doubling the divisor and doubling the multiple it represents together always stay consistent, if temp_divisor is currently k times the original divisor, doubling both keeps that same k-to-1 relationship, so subtracting temp_divisor and crediting multiple to the quotient is always mathematically exact, never an approximation. Repeating this find-the-biggest-fitting-chunk process across multiple outer passes correctly accounts for every part of the dividend, since each pass strictly reduces what remains until it drops below the divisor entirely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The remaining dividend is still at least the divisor","A new inner doubling search finds the largest chunk that fits, that chunk is subtracted, and its multiple is added to the quotient","The quotient grows by a large, exact amount each outer pass"],["The remaining dividend has dropped below the divisor","No further division fits","The outer loop ends and the quotient is complete"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The inner loop's condition checks the next doubling, dividend against temp_divisor shifted one more time, before committing to double, so temp_divisor only ever grows to the largest value that still fits within the current remaining dividend.
multiple doubles in lockstep with temp_divisor on every inner iteration, since it exists purely to track how many original divisors the current temp_divisor represents.

The outer while loop repeats the entire doubling search from scratch each time, starting temp_divisor back at the plain divisor, since the remaining dividend has shrunk and the previous chunk size may no longer be the largest one that fits.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: roughly O(log squared of the dividend), a dramatic improvement over the brute force for extreme inputs, since each outer pass removes at least half of what remains relative to the divisor.
Space: O(1).
10. Further Optimization: One Pass Over the Bits

The doubling approach still has a nested loop, an outer loop for each pass and an inner loop to find how far to double. The same idea can be restructured into a single, clean pass: walk through each bit position of a 32 bit number from the highest down to the lowest, and directly decide whether that bit belongs in the quotient.
Dry run for dividend = 43, divisor = 3

blocks.text: The quotient with bits 3, 2, and 1 set is 8 + 4 + 2 = 14, matching the doubling approach exactly, but built in a single, direct pass over the bit positions.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: decide each bit of the quotient directly, from highest to lowest

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The loop walks bit positions from 31 down to 0, from most significant to least significant, since deciding the largest bits of the quotient first is what allows each subsequent, smaller bit decision to work against a correctly reduced remaining dividend.

Shifting dividend right by bit before comparing to divisor is a quick way to test whether divisor, shifted left by bit, fits in dividend, without risking an intermediate overflow from shifting divisor left too far first.
Setting the bit in quotient and subtracting divisor shifted left by that same bit are two sides of the same decision, made together only when that bit position's chunk of the divisor actually fits.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), a fixed number of bit positions for a standard integer, effectively O(1) and a cleaner single pass than the nested doubling loop.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is building the answer bit by bit, from the most significant position down to the least, which shows up repeatedly whenever a quantity needs to be constructed under a constraint that forbids multiplication or division directly. Doubling based chunk subtraction and single pass bit construction are really two views of the exact same underlying idea.
Common Mistakes

items: Flooring instead of truncating toward zero for negative results, which gives the wrong answer for cases like 7 divided by -3.

Forgetting the classic overflow edge case: dividing the most negative possible integer by -1 overflows, since its positive equivalent cannot be represented in the same integer type, this needs an explicit guard.
Using multiplication or division accidentally while computing the sign or intermediate values, defeating the point of the exercise.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is a strong test of bit manipulation fluency under an artificial constraint. Moving from naive repeated subtraction, to doubling based chunk removal, to a single clean pass over the bits, demonstrates the same kind of layered optimization thinking that shows up across many bit manipulation interview questions.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "you cannot use multiply or divide", think: bit shifts double and halve values without ever calling those operators.
If the interviewer says "can you do better than repeated subtraction", think: double the chunk being subtracted for as long as it still fits.
If the interviewer says "can you do this in a single pass", think: decide each bit of the quotient directly, from the highest bit down to the lowest.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does doubling based chunk subtraction run in roughly log squared time, rather than plain logarithmic time?
Can you explain why the single pass bit construction approach avoids the nested loop entirely?
What specific input causes integer overflow in this problem, and how do you guard against it?
How would this approach change if you needed to support arbitrarily large integers, not fixed 32-bit ones?
Can you adapt this same bit-by-bit construction idea to implement multiplication instead of division, without using the multiply operator?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "implement basic arithmetic without the usual operator" problem, multiplication, square root, or exponentiation built from bit shifts and additions, which reuses this same chunk-doubling or bit-by-bit construction idea.
Fast exponentiation, Pow(x, n), which uses the same halving and doubling relationship, just applied to repeated multiplication instead of repeated subtraction.
Binary representation construction problems in general, where a result is built one bit position at a time, from most significant to least significant.

Overflow-aware arithmetic, since this problem's classic edge case, the most negative integer divided by -1, reappears in any problem involving negation or absolute value near the limits of a fixed width integer type.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Repeated subtraction runs in O(dividend divided by divisor) time, which can be catastrophically slow for extreme inputs. Doubling based chunk subtraction brings this down to roughly O(log squared of the dividend). The single pass bit construction approach reaches the cleanest result, a fixed O(32) pass, effectively O(1) for standard integers, with O(1) space throughout every version.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: building the quotient bit by bit, using doubling and bit shifts to remove large chunks of the dividend at once, all without multiplication, division, or modulo.

Core Idea: a bit shift doubles a value without ever calling multiply, so the divisor can be doubled repeatedly to find the largest chunk that still fits the remaining dividend, and this same idea can be restructured into directly deciding each bit of the quotient, from most significant to least.
Time: O(dividend divided by divisor) for the brute force, roughly O(log squared of the dividend) for doubling chunk subtraction, O(32), effectively O(1), for the single pass bit construction.
Space: O(1) across every version.

Most Important Observation: forbidding multiplication and division does not forbid doubling and halving, bit shifts provide exactly that power, and that alone is enough to reach a near-constant-time solution.

Interview Difficulty: easy to write the correct but catastrophically slow brute force; the doubling refinement and especially the single pass bit construction are what demonstrate real bit manipulation fluency.
One line memory trick: double the chunk, or just decide each bit directly, never subtract one copy at a time.
